Due to the optical cable's properties, the signal experienced significant distortions, resulting in four spectral nulls that severely impacted the system's performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially used, but it had a major drawback: it propagated errors when the signal encountered unstable conditions. Fortunately, combining a weighted DFE with maximum likelihood sequence estimation was found to be highly effective in eliminating distortions and achieving the best possible correction rate of 10^-4. Networks (TCNs) are well-suited for processing time-series data. However, optimizing the time-dilated convolution in TCNs typically involves a trial-and-error approach. We've developed an automatic optimizer that tackles this challenge by treating dilation factor selection as a weight pruning problem on the time-axis. Our method learns dilation factors alongside model weights during training, leading to significant reductions in model size and inference latency on real hardware by up to 7.4x and 3x respectively, without compromising accuracy. Additionally, it enables the discovery of multiple pruned models from a single original TCN model, outperforming manual optimization in both model size and accuracy.

massive arc-like structure on the sky at a redshift of approximately 0.8. Spanning nearly 1 gigaparsec in proper size at the present epoch, this 'Giant Arc' appears almost symmetrical on the sky. It was discovered using a novel approach that involves examining the spectra of background quasars for intervening magnesium II absorbers, with the goal of investigating its properties and potential associations with large-scale structure. We present the observational data and various analyses, including magnitudes and likelihood of collision between matter and light, which suggest the Giant Arc is a massive, elongated feature. using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has gained significant attention. Two main categories of approaches have emerged: direct methods and two-stage pipelines that utilize intermediate cues. In the latter category, the first stage involves CNN regression of cues such as 3D object coordinates or virtual control points. These intermediate cues are then used to construct correspondence constraints, ultimately facilitating the computation of object pose. This paper focuses on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct strategies: cross-stage augmentation and boundary point prioritization. We employ these strategies to enhance the training of boundary-detecting CNNs, ultimately achieving pose estimation accuracy superior to that of existing methods. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of these proposals and their integration into various two-stage pipelines. Furthermore, we find that the networks we train using these methods can be applied to scenarios where only a single image is available, significantly outperforming previous works that also utilize additional data from the same category.

Bond-Based Peridynamics, despite its limitations, has become a widely used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation and intuitive connection to real-world phenomena. This paper reviews and examines various aspects of bond-based peridynamic models, providing a detailed overview and critical analysis of the literature. The underlying mechanics and mathematics of these models are discussed, including their differences and commonalities, as well as the implications of their varying bond potentials on the resulting PD integral kernels. Further, the paper highlights the role of interstitial water in governing the velocity of brittle fracture and presents new evidence using a Sandwell fringe analysis. Finally, the influence of BB-PD's kinematic and potential assumptions on its ability to capture fracture patterns is summarized and presented in the context of a new perspective.

designed to solve General Graphical Lasso problems. The Graphical Lasso approach, initially introduced by Friedman in 2007 and later developed by others, estimates a sparse inverse covariance matrix from multivariate Gaussian data. This framework, originally proposed by Dempster in 1972 under the name Covariance Selection, has been expanded to accommodate latent variables, as shown in Chandrasekaran's 2012 work. More recent advancements include the joint estimation of multiple inverse covariance matrices, as demonstrated in Danaher's 2013 and Tomasi's 2018 studies. The GGLasso package offers methods for solving a wide range of General Graphical Lasso problems, encompassing various special cases, as outlined in the reference paper available under an open-source license.

By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, researchers can now quantify sampling errors and determine time steps independently of the system size. For harmonic oscillators, some methods yield exact results, allowing for the optimal choice of sampling methods to be identified. In more complex systems, the best approach is to match the step size for deterministic forces and drifts. However, this may not always be the case, and further development of better methods is still possible. The results also highlight the benefits of using the velocity version of these methods over their positional counterparts. Additionally, this study introduces a new factorization that can be used to create more efficient variants of existing algorithms. Finally, the accuracy of these algorithms is verified through their implementation in the AMD Lena molecular system.

However, these simulations start relatively close to the merger, so it's essential to determine the initial conditions that accurately represent the binary and its environment at this point. In our research, we've been investigating how dark matter behaves around equal-mass black hole binaries, discovering a stable, long-lasting profile that emerges and grows as the binary evolves. Conversely, heavier dark matter tends to be displaced by the binary's motion. As simulations progress, different initial setups eventually converge to the preferred profile, but they may also introduce unwanted oscillations, which can affect short simulation runs. Furthermore, simply adding matter to a circular binary can lead to artificially eccentric orbits, making it crucial to carefully choose the initial conditions to avoid misinterpreting dark matter effects. Since the preferred profile is stable, further refinement of initial conditions may not be necessary, and we can also use it to inform future simulations of dark matter binaries.

In our approach, a network with multiple weighted and potentially directed graphs is analyzed, where each graph represents a single network layer without any inter-layer connections. Through the examination of extensive categories of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we identify the potential generalized global symmetries present and investigate the mechanisms by which they are circumvented. Key components of such effective field theories include generalized $\theta$-terms, which introduce non-linear interactions between axion fields and topological terms that are quadratic in gauge field strengths and which break a substantial portion of the global symmetries. Moreover, assuming the presence of charged states can lead to the further breakdown of residual global symmetries. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that the presence of generalized $\theta$-terms results in a generalized Witten effect, implying that the spectrum of charged states is composed of an infinitely populated grid. Furthermore, we show that this grid is generated by the action of the monodromy transformation that characterizes the boundary of the moduli space near which the effective theory is defined.

  Our objective is to minimize the number and intricacy of hardware and software components that a mobile user must trust to withstand malicious inputs. We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware design, consisting of isolated, statically-partitioned trust domains, and a simple, user-controllable hardware mechanism to reallocate this static partitioning as needed. This mechanism is powered by a straightforward, formally-verified software system.
  As an example, our design integrates a microcontroller and screen with two trust domains: one for the operating system and another for a verified security application. When a user downloads a new program, they can choose to run it in an untrusted code domain, which the user and verified applications can monitor from a safe distance. This untrusted code can access system resources solely through a transparent, automatically-generated, and safely-contained hardware module (HM).
  Our hardware and software trust minimal components by utilizing an extension to traditional hardware and software co-design, and a novel holistic security through hardware and software co-rotation. We have implemented our design on a system incorporating an nRF52840 chip and a screen, and our results show that the untrusted code domain incurs a minor performance cost and limited area overhead compared to a single-trust-domain system.

Our adversary model assumes a sophisticated opponent who can manipulate the reward and transition at any step within an episode, but only up to a certain percentage of episodes. Our model is more aggressive than previous approaches. We initially demonstrated that no algorithm can find a significantly better policy than one that is slightly suboptimal, given our attack model. Notably, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can maintain robustness if the reward corruption is limited, and can find a near-optimal policy. To address unbounded reward corruption, we developed the Filtered Policy Gradient algorithm, which can find a nearly optimal policy despite significant corruption. We also showed that a neural implementation of FPG can achieve strong robust learning performance on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks.

multi-phonon physics, is being explored for its potential in metrology and on-chip communication, among other applications. Quantum acoustic resonators, or cavities, are being utilized to investigate multi-phonon phenomena both theoretically and experimentally. We investigate a system consisting of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity. This system has exhibited intriguing multi-phonon effects, and previous studies attempted to explain it using a two-level quantum dot model. However, we demonstrate that using a three-level quantum dot model, specifically with the excitation of a satellite energy level, the emission of a multi-phonon mode can be achieved with a lower laser frequency than previously thought. This could lead to the creation of a multi-phonon device with a lower threshold and better efficiency.

lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying different potentials to the two sublattices, or introduce small inequivalent displacements along the principal lattice directions. As a result of these transformations, the Dirac cones are transformed near the projected time-reversal symmetry points from which they become quasi-flat along high-symmetry lines within the first Brillouin zone. Additionally, we outline a potential implementation of this model using CO atoms on a Cu(111) surface. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that this system could display non-symmorphic topological properties, which might be recognized through the observation of a specific, non-trivial Chern number along a high-symmetry path.

yzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated through a process called quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a specific photon count is detected in a specific output channel. We demonstrate that SPCCSs exhibit sub-Poisson statistics and elastically scatter photons, making them useful for studying single-photon avalance photodiodes and determining the purity of squeezed states. To date, SPCCSs have been produced using parametric amplifiers and single-photon sources, such as spontaneous parametric down-conversion and spontaneous emission from a two-level atom. We also investigate the production of SPCCSs using a Kerr amplifier and a correlated coherent state.

CT scans can be very difficult due to low contrast, varying anatomy, and the presence of foreign objects. To compensate for these challenges, doctors often rely on additional information from endoscopic findings, medical history, and other imaging tests, which can be time-consuming and produce inconsistent results. This study investigates the potential of a simplified clinical workflow that uses a deep learning system to automatically segment esophageal tumors from CT scans. The research team collected a large dataset of 2880 CT scans with corresponding masks and developed a fully automated segmentation model called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. To test the model's robustness, it was trained with data from multiple centers and with different scanning devices. The results show that the model achieves high accuracy and can process scans quickly, at a rate of over 300 scans per minute. Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis confirms that the model's performance is consistent across different training data balances and spatial resolution levels. This innovative model has the potential to streamline the diagnosis process and provide fast and reliable tumor segmentations for clinicians.

This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in an iterative process is often part of a geosteering workflow. Our approach combines a nonlinear inversion strategy, specifically Luke's method, in conjunction with a Tikhonov regularization technique, to enforce stability. We also utilize an Adam optimization method to handle the challenge of convergence. The proposed formulation is designed to enable real-time computations on regular CPUs. To verify the performance of this approach, we used two synthetic cases featuring diverse reservoir properties and five different logging tools. The results showed that these models were successfully matched with their corresponding measurements. Additionally, we analyzed the effect of decreasing the regularization parameter and the number of optimization iterations on the accuracy of the formation evaluation. The findings indicated that the formation evaluations retain their accuracy even when the inversion is partially converged.

In this study, we explore zero-shot and few-shot transfer of NER knowledge across languages and discover that transferring knowledge from a resource-rich language to a resource-poor one does not always yield positive results due to differing character distributions and over-reliance on domain-specific knowledge. problems involving arithmetic, such as the $\mathbb{A}^1$-counting of bitangents to plane quartics with values in the Grothendieck-Witt ring, and rationality over valued fields, with a focus on using bitangents to quartics as a test case. We investigate quartic curves over valued fields whose tropical forms are smooth and satisfy a mild genericity condition. We express the obstacles to the rationality of bitangents and their points of tangency in terms of edge twisting of the tropical form; this twisting is determined solely by the tropical form and the initial coefficients of the defining equation, up to squares. We demonstrate that the GW-multiplicity of a tropical bitangent, i.e., the multiplicity with which its lifts contribute to the $\mathbb{A}^1$-counting of bitangents, can be calculated from the tropical form of the quartic and the initial coefficients of the defining equation. As a consequence, we show that the four lifts of most tropical bitangent classes contribute $2\mathbb{H}$ to the $\mathbb{A}^1$-counting, providing evidence for a conjecture of Larson and Vogt on the $\mathbb{A}^1$-counting of bitangents over the reals.

Code-switching often occurs in multilingual speakers, where they seamlessly transition between languages within a single conversation or written text. This study examines the current state of natural language processing research, highlighting its limitations and potential drawbacks in addressing five critical areas for the greater good: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, misinformation, and hate speech in multilingual communities. To drive progress in multilingual NLP applications, we suggest the development of innovative datasets and models that can significantly improve code-switching research. To achieve this, we propose training monolingual and multilingual models using similar datasets and models, before testing their performance on real-world cases.

Microwave Background (CMB) could be evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology (CCC) model, which proposes the universe undergoes cycles of expansion and contraction. These patterns include low-variance circles resulting from black hole mergers and Hawking points resulting from black hole evaporation. A recent study used machine learning software called HawkingNet to search for Hawking points in the CMB, but found no statistically significant evidence. Similarly, a high-resolution search for low-variance circles in the Planck and WMAP CMB data revealed no significant results after removing anomalies. However, the absence of distinct features in the CMB does not necessarily disprove CCC, as a large density of such patterns could produce a non-Gaussian fluctuation in the CMB. Interestingly, the real CMB sky exhibits significant local deviations from Gaussian noise on a local scale, according to the best-fit Lambda-CDM and COM PowerSpect CBM TT-full power spectra.

To achieve the necessary sensitivity for planet detection and to enable the accurate characterization of substellar companions, it is essential to accurately model the activity noise in these stars. We also investigated alternative models and novel approaches to assess the uncertainty in the activity model fit. Our primary finding is that the activity model with an added Gaussian process component provides the best fit to the data and yields the most accurate short-term activity predictions. We conclude that incorporating a Gaussian process component is a logical approach to modeling M dwarfs' active regions and their rotation cycles. We provide a publicly accessible code to estimate activity noise for M dwarfs in real-time, which can be used to model activity noise in individual stars and account for the effect in the data fit.

Infective to Recovered (SIR) epidemic model on a social network is conducted. The social network, represented by an Erdos-Renyi random graph, undergoes changes as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours drop or rewire their connections during the epidemic. The model's large population limits are derived, yielding convergence results for the initial branching process-like behavior and the main epidemic phase, which converges to a deterministic model equivalent to a specific pair approximation model. Additionally, law of large numbers results are obtained for the final size of a major outbreak. Two key findings emerge: (i) the limiting fraction of infected individuals may exhibit a discontinuous jump from 0 to a positive value at the infection rate's threshold, and (ii) when rewiring occurs to uninfected individuals, the limiting fraction of infected individuals jumps from 0 to 1 as the infection rate passes through its threshold.

structures of iron-based superconductors is crucial for developing microscopic theories on their superconductivity mechanisms. However, even for extensively studied compounds like (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, there remain uncertainties regarding their electronic and superconducting gap structures. Our study addresses these issues by employing high-resolution ARPES measurements on (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ using both Helium lamps and laser light sources. Our results reveal that the observed "flat band" feature near the Brillouin zone center in the superconducting state arises from the combined effects of superconductivity-induced band back-bending and band folding from the zone corner to the center. Furthermore, we have directly observed band folding between the zone corner and center in both the normal and superconducting states, allowing for the accurate assignment of bands and the determination of a small band exposure at the zone center in both states. Near the zone corner, we have observed a minima on a dispersive M-shaped band in both states and have measured a relatively large gap size of approximately 8 meV. These findings have led to the establishment of a new superconducting gap map around the zone corner and have implications for understanding the superconductivity mechanism in iron-based superconductors.

These clusters exhibit distinct and complex dynamics when compared to on-site clusters in non-interacting particle systems. This study introduces a new method to indirectly identify ultra-high energy photons by observing the interaction between photons and cosmic rays between the Sun and the Earth. A comprehensive simulation of this process, called the 'Sun lens,' has been developed using the GEANT4 code. This phenomenon involves the redirection of ultra-high energy photons towards the Earth by cosmic ray nuclei, with energies exceeding 10^18 eV and angles smaller than a few milliradians. The simulation has been implemented in a way that allows for the inclusion of new primary photon events in ultra-high energy cosmic ray data sets. The expected event rates are on the order of 10^8 to 10^9 below 10^19 eV, and as low as 10^7 at 10^20 eV. The observed multi-energy spectrum would indicate an additional component of photons, accounting for 10% to 30% of the total flux between 10^18 and 10^20 eV. The simulation has been incorporated into the UHEA-III code package, enabling the simulation of ultra-high energy photon data sets and the comparison with experimental data in the future.

The nonlocal aspect in this theory is influenced by past events through a specific relationship involving a causal factor. This relationship differs from Einstein's gravity, making it analogous to nonlocal electrodynamics where the permittivity varies with distance. In nonlocal gravity, the causal factor is modeled as a function of an infrared cutoff, similar to nonlocal electrodynamics. This choice enables a direct comparison with the Spacetime Foam model. Both models display similarities in behavior. Additionally, both theories exhibit features that are consistent with current gravitational wave observations. It's also possible to connect the strength of nonlocality in gravity to experimental data, much like nonlocal electrodynamics.

To achieve this consistency, leaders and followers must adhere to strict rules or take responsibility for errors. the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered.

To assess the feasibility of this test, I employed a specific method that involves analyzing only the velocity components within a specific plane. This analysis was applied to a computational model of the Milky Way, taking into account the uncertainty in stellar position. The results showed that the velocity dispersion of binary star velocities, as determined using a simple statistical method, is relatively unaffected by the direction of the galactic flow. However, the same model failed to validate this test when the velocity data was analyzed using a more complex statistical method, or when the orientation of the velocity field was varied. Furthermore, my analysis revealed that the uncertainty in binary star velocity is significantly influenced by the inclination of their line of sight, due to the random orientation of their velocity vectors. As a result, binary star velocities offer a promising test of the law of gravity, but only if the data is analyzed appropriately and the uncertainty is accounted for in a way that depends on the inclination of the line of sight.

-mass stellar objects may be impacted by rotation due to the influence of centrifugal force on their equilibrium and the possibility of mass loss through rotational break-up. We have created numerical models of rotating low-mass stars to examine their ability to sustain nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates that result in significant deformation. Critical boundaries defining the conditions for sustainable hydrogen burning have been identified in terms of mass and central degeneracy for various levels of angular momentum. Our findings indicate that when the angular momentum surpasses a certain threshold, the critical boundary splits into two distinct regions with lower and higher degeneracy due to mass loss. Based on these results, we have modeled the thermal and mechanical evolution of substellar objects, taking into account mass loss, which occurs when the centrifugal radius exceeds the stellar radius. This model is applied to two scenarios: one with external cooling, which determines the mass function $M_{\rm c}(M)$, and the other with internal heating, which determines the birth rate function $R_{\rm h}(M)$. Additionally, we have estimated the number of objects that undergo mass loss due to rotation and have constructed a simple model for the observed luminosity function of brown dwarfs, taking into account their mass function.

groups of objects have numerous practical applications and are often represented graphically as a 2-tier layout, where each group is displayed as a set of nodes on separate horizontal lines, and the relationships between them are depicted by lines connecting corresponding nodes on the two lines. One key goal in creating these visualizations is to minimize the number of intersecting lines, but achieving this is computationally intensive and may still result in cluttered layouts that compromise their clarity. We explore a recent method to eliminate these intersections by relocating nodes, aiming to identify the minimum number of nodes that need to be relocated to produce an uncluttered layout. Our research demonstrates that determining whether a clear layout can be achieved by relocating no more than $k$ nodes is computationally efficient in relation to $k$.

research introduces a new technique called HyperDegrade, which combines existing methods with the use of multi-threading architectures.  In addition to this new technique, the study identifies the underlying causes of performance degradation through cache eviction and uncovers a previously unknown source of slowdown. The resulting slowdown is significantly higher than previous methods, leading to a finer time granularity for Flush+Reload attacks. The effectiveness of HyperDegrade is demonstrated on various Intel microarchitectures, resulting in a finer time granularity of three orders of magnitude for data reloads and two orders of magnitude for cache line flushes. To further illustrate the technique's efficacy, a case study is conducted on an OpenSSL benchmark, showcasing how HyperDegrade can leverage existing vulnerabilities to produce a performance degradation of up to 17 times at a much finer granularity than previously attainable. Moreover, through Flush+Reload attacks on two CPUs, the study demonstrates the capability to guess 68% of 128-bit secrets with an average of around 2200 trials per secret.

explain the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, we employed an Effective Field Theory (EFT) approach. Although the Standard Model (SM) contribution of the Higgs to the muon's magnetic dipole moment is minimal, a bottom-up EFT analysis reveals that the Higgs could still provide a viable solution to the anomaly, given current experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, if its interactions with other SM particles deviate from SM predictions. Applying unitarity principles, we found that such a solution would imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of around 10-18 TeV, which could be lowered to 5 TeV if the Higgs interactions with W and Z bosons conform to SM expectations. This scenario could lead to a significant increase in di-Higgs production in muon colliders, making it a compelling reason to investigate further. Ultimately, our study underscores the importance of measuring the coupling between the Higgs boson and two muons in future experiments.

Fields like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning heavily rely on matrices to solve their respective problems.
Given the frequency of matrix operations, efficient matrix handling is crucial for algorithm performance.

study, we concentrate on vertical federated learning (VFL), which allows multiple entities to jointly train a robust machine learning model using shared features, without exchanging sensitive information. Based on collaboration patterns, VFL can be distinguished from horizontal federated learning. Our focus is on identifying potential privacy breaches in real-world VFL systems. To achieve this, we have developed and implemented two real-world privacy attacks: a reverse multiplication attack targeting the logistic regression VFL protocol, and a reverse sum attack targeting the XGBoost VFL protocol. Our empirical results demonstrate that the attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and easy to execute, even when intermediate outputs are encrypted. The leaked information can be used to train a new classifier that performs as well as the original model. We also investigate potential countermeasures and their challenges, as well as potential avenues for future research.

Tetralogy of Fallot patients primarily relies on ventricular volume and function according to current clinical guidelines. These biomarkers can be accurately assessed through 3D cardiac magnetic resonance image segmentation. Recent studies have shown a model that estimates these biomarkers directly from whole-heart images performs better than conventional two-segmentation approaches. Nonetheless, such models overlook crucial information present in images outside the main ventricles and heart muscles. Furthermore, they often fail to provide confidence limits for their predictions, which is crucial for clinical decision-making. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach that incorporates more image context and outputs probability distributions of predictions. This approach, based on a attention-based neural network architecture, outperforms existing two-segmentation methods according to certain evaluation metrics. Moreover, our method segments multiple organs simultaneously while predicting cardiovascular biomarkers. In line with clinical practices, we also present models that output confidence limits alongside biomarker predictions, which are made publicly available for researchers and clinicians to use.

Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors.

These tools allow us to derive explicit formulas for approximating extreme cases of a specific type of model, including the distribution of a tail event and a key metric of asymptotic independence. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. Our findings show that these models not only perform much worse than humans but also struggle to efficiently use the information provided by visual data. The annealed large deviation principle for the empirical process of words involves a rate function that is the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of words relative to the reference distribution of words. In a previous study, the quenched large deviation principle was derived for renewal times that are independently and identically distributed, resulting in a rate function that includes both the annealed rate function and the rate function associated with the exchangeable partition model. When the number of letters goes to infinity, both rate functions converge to zero. It was demonstrated that the convergence of the rate functions to zero is characterized by the condition that the second moment of the renewal times is finite. This condition was previously proven necessary, and it is now shown that it is also sufficient.

A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger, detect, and isolate faults. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each program failure. This study applies an innovative mutation analysis approach to fuzzing, combining multiple mutations to increase the detectability of faults and reducing the required independent evaluations by means of cross-validation. The evaluation of fuzzers is conducted on Zephyr, a widely used operating system, and compares the enhanced approach with existing techniques. The evaluation is based on existing fuzzers for various protocols and file formats, and the results demonstrate the limitations of contemporary fuzzers using the commonly applied metrics. The introduced evaluation framework and the defined mutation models are made publicly available.

Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing minimal updates or no updates to the backbone models during the training process. In this study, we investigate whether the complexity of these models is truly necessary for achieving optimal performance by comparing them to a basic alternative we have designed. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can be a robust tool for achieving competitive or even superior continual learning results on the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted a straightforward baseline that 1) employs a frozen pre-trained model to extract image features for each class encountered during the continual learning stage and computes the corresponding mean features from the training data, and 2) predicts the class of the input based on the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and the mean features of the classes; that is, the Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This baseline is single-headed, exemplar-free, and can be task-free and achieves 88.53% on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100, outperforming most state-of-the-art continual learning methods that are all built upon the complexity of deep neural networks. Our baseline validates the counter-intuitive idea that a deep learning model can be a continual learning masterpiece even without any neural network components.

and Shmaya introduced a category of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games where each player's payoff function is influenced by a $\lambda$-Lipschitz rate in response to other players' actions. Their work demonstrated that these types of games possess a Nash equilibrium with optimal second-order, smooth payoffs in a $\lambda$-ball centered at zero. The current study expands upon their findings by relaxing the Lipschitz condition to $\lambda$-Lipschitz while also incorporating action space. We established a novel inequality indicating that any $\lambda$-Lipschitz game contains a Nash equilibrium within a $\lambda$-Hölder class over the entire action space. Furthermore, we presented an upper bound for the distance between the game's Nash equilibrium and a base game that is zero for the bi-exponential function when the number of players increases to the power of two and for the double-well potential function when the number of players increases to the power of three. Additionally, this study investigates two scenarios of multi-player games that converge to zero or reach a steady-state as the number of players grows indefinitely.

Yet, this CV process relies on random data partitioning, yielding stochastic performance estimates with considerable variability, particularly in natural language processing. This instability renders CV estimates unreliable for parameter tuning, as the selected parameters are highly susceptible to the partitioning method, often resulting in suboptimal choices and significant reproducibility issues. In contrast, we suggest utilizing the less variable J-k-fold CV approach, which involves conducting J independent k-fold cross-validations to evaluate model performance. Our contributions include adapting J-k-fold CV to parameter tuning and investigating optimal J and k values. We contend that minimizing variability is more crucial than minimizing bias for effective parameter tuning, and therefore recommend lower k values and increased J to conserve computational resources. To validate our suggestions, we conduct a comprehensive analysis across multiple classification and sentiment analysis datasets, using various models and evaluating model performance through mean squad error. The results provide guidelines for using J-k-fold CV with randomness for efficient parameter tuning.

a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction were optimally determined through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in image analysis. Optimal reconstruction parameters were found through visual assessment and metric aggregation. Spatial resolution and contrast were improved from $4.46mm$ and $34.61$ to $3.36mm$ and $41.03$ by adjusting reconstruction parameters. A quantitative analysis of motion compensation showed a 94.19% success rate in identifying image-forming data and estimating deformation fields with an error of $1.441mm$. This new rCASPR-based method for generating motion-compensated 4D MRI allows for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI.

This phenomenon reaches its maximum intensity at a specific temperature and magnetic field strength, which likely corresponds to the point where the entropy difference between the central region of the vortex and its surroundings is most pronounced. Notably, the magnitude of this peak is strikingly consistent across a wide range of superconducting materials, suggesting a common underlying mechanism. This peak can be interpreted as the point at which the ratio of viscosity to entropy density within the vortex liquid is minimized. When expressed in terms of the superfluid density of the material, this minimum takes on a more physically interpretable form. Furthermore, the superconducting phase of the heavy fermion material UBe$_{13}$ is found to exhibit a similar peak in its thermal conductivity when the influence of the Fermi liquid instabilities within the normal state is taken into account. As a result, a more comprehensive understanding of this phenomenon can be gained, taking into account both many-body effects and quantum fluctuations.

Current methods of assessing this flexibility are often based on slow-moving estimations, with less attention paid to real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem in a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism called maximum entropy feedback (MEF). As the interacting stars move closer together, either through the transfer of material or a close approach, the envelope's interaction determines their final fate. This phase can result in a variety of outcomes, including mergers, subsequent interactions, and potentially observable events. We explore the potential mergers of a black hole and neutron star in the context of a common envelope, using both analytical models and simulations to understand their dynamics. It is predicted that the increased gravitational pull causes the neutron star to spiral towards the black hole and eventually become engulfed. If the neutron star's mass remains below a certain threshold as it heats up, a significant portion of its mass could be converted into energy, potentially resulting in a highly energetic electromagnetic explosion. Furthermore, our findings suggest that in certain scenarios, the final merger could take the form of a standard or hypernovae explosion, being detectable in various ways. It is also possible that the neutron star's mass conversion could lead to the detection of a gravitational wave signal in certain situations.

Using cylindrical objects of varying lengths and diameters, and grains made of materials with either high or low friction, we measured the drag forces acting on the object in different directions as it moved through the grain bed at various speeds. Our results show that the drag experienced by the object varies significantly depending on its orientation, the speed at which it is moving, and the ratio of its length to its diameter. Specifically, we found that the drag experienced by the object when it is oriented perpendicular to its axis is significantly greater than when it is oriented parallel to its axis, and that this difference in drag increases as the speed of the object increases and as the length of the object increases relative to its diameter. Furthermore, we found that the drag experienced by the object is consistent with the idea that the flow of grains around the object is dominated by frictional forces, and that the shape of the object plays a significant role in determining the drag it experiences.

we've analyzed the large-scale structure of ionized and molecular gas in the starbursting galaxy IRAS08339+6517, located 500 parsecs in size. Our study has uncovered a direct relationship between the mass flux of star formation-driven gas outflows and the galaxy's star formation rate. The data suggest that outflows are closely linked to the galaxy's ability to recycle gas, with areas of high star formation rates expelling more gas than they consume through star formation. These findings support the idea that outflows play a crucial role in regulating the galaxy's ability to sustain short gas depletion times. Our results highlight the importance of further studies on gas outflows in galaxies to better understand their role in galaxy evolution.

Recently, Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO) has successfully addressed these issues by utilizing probabilistic models. SBO achieves fast convergence by breaking down the parameter space using contextual information from system experts. However, the complexity of building probabilistic models has limited its widespread adoption. To overcome this hurdle, we introduce BoAnon, a SBO framework that learns system structure from logs. BoAnon offers an API for experts to incorporate system knowledge as performance models or component dependencies. By combining the learned structure with expert-provided knowledge, BoAnon creates a probabilistic graph model that enables the optimizer to discover efficient configurations more quickly than other methods. In a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a significant improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. BoAnon's innovative approach to contextual structure learning makes SBO more accessible for a variety of computer systems, including databases and stream processors.

Our research focuses on the early stages of superbubble evolution, including pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae. We aimed to investigate the growth of dust grains within orbiting dusty clumps and the superbubble's swept-up supershell, as well as the survival of dust grains produced by sequential supernovae. Our model takes into account the gravitational potential of the star cluster and the self-gravity of the parent cloud, as well as radiative cooling and a state-of-the-art population synthesis model for the coeval cluster. Our findings show that in massive molecular clouds hosting a super star cluster, dust grain growth increases the dust mass at a rate of approximately 4.8 times 10 to the negative 5 solar masses per year during the first 2.5 million years. Furthermore, pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae contribute significantly to the superbubble's supershell, resulting in the deposition of massive amounts of dust produced by sequential supernovae. This process results in the supershell becoming an important reservoir of dust, with a dust mass equivalent to approximately 10 percent of the parent cloud's initial dust mass. Our model's predictions are compared with those of other theoretical models and observational data, and we conclude that superbubbles in low-metallicity molecular clouds have the potential to explain the widespread distribution of heavy elements and dust observed in galaxies.

However, existing benchmarks, such as the nuScenes dataset, do not adequately address this problem as they only evaluate performance up to a certain distance. This is partly due to the difficulty in obtaining far-field 3D annotations, particularly from lidar sensors that often produce few point returns for distant objects. Moreover, current evaluation protocols for Far-field 3D detection are unsatisfactory as they simply use a fixed distance threshold, which is often arbitrary and may not reflect the practical needs of autonomous braking systems. For instance, the nuScenes benchmark uses a 50% FSDTR (False Positive Suppressed Detection Rate) protocol, which has been shown to lead to inconsistent and unstable rankings. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel FSD evaluation protocol that for the first time uses the projected ground plane density of detected objects for evaluation, which better reflects the practical needs of Far-field 3D detection for autonomous braking systems. We also propose an effective far-field 3D detection evaluation protocol and a state-of-the-art method for Far-field 3D detection, called Multi-resolution Fusion (MF), which has consistently outperformed all other methods in various settings. The code for our method and evaluation protocol is available at https://github.com/autointell/mf_fsd.git.

Nevertheless, calculating this data is a complex task due to the need to sample a vast number of ground states across the high-dimensional PES. In this research, we introduce a novel approach using a generative quantum machine learning model to prepare quantum states at any point on the PES. Our method employs a classical neural network to correct the annealing schedule of a quantum neural network, ensuring that the parameters align with the optimal classical data. We confirm that a single parameter shift is sufficient to connect points on the PES by demonstrating the quantum-classical nature of our protocol. Furthermore, we utilize a classical optimizer to identify the best schedule for achieving superconducting quantum annealing on a bucket reactor decomposition scenario. Our experiments with both simulated and real-world data, as well as a 52-qubit quantum processor, reveal that the quantum-classical protocol enhances the efficiency of quantum annealing, showing a 50-fold improvement in success rate at a specific point on the PES. This technique may facilitate the utilization of quantum annealing devices by enabling the preparation of quantum states for practical applications.

For laparoscopic liver surgery, we align the preoperative CT scan model with the intraoperative partial organ surface reconstructed from laparoscopic video, despite the difficulties posed by sparse, noisy, real-time, and uncertain data, such as tissue properties and boundary conditions. Our experiments demonstrate the network's ability to translate to real data while achieving fast and stable convergence during inference. The developed model exhibits high potential for real-world application and sets a new direction for learning-based correspondence and registration.

We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. This concept, initially explored in the 1970s, combines properties of matchings, Hamiltonian cycles, and edge colourings. This study focuses on cubic graphs and aims to identify those where every perfect matching corresponds to a colour in a proper 3-edge-colouring. This is equivalent to determining whether such graphs are even-2-factorable, meaning all their 2-factors consist solely of even cycles. Since bipartite cubic graphs are trivially even-2-factorable, we concentrate on non-bipartite cubic graphs. A cubic graph with the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property is a sufficient but not necessary condition for being even-2-factorable. This work introduces a family of even-2-factorable non-bipartite cubic graphs, known as papillon graphs, and examines the parameters for which these graphs possess the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property or are simply even-2-factorable. Additionally, we prove that papillon graphs with different parameters are never isomorphic.

Two alternative methods, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as potential solutions. WRI inverts wavefield time samples and/or frequency components, while ESI uses extended sources to match observed data and wavefield records. This study formulates both WRI and ESI within a unified mathematical framework and compares them to FWI. Formulas for the matrices involved in these methods are derived, and their relationships are discussed. An important characteristic of these methods is that they relate the data residual to the wavefield and source or receiver information. As such, they can be viewed as parametric linearized versions of FWI, with different forms determined by the chosen time-frequency source characteristics. To validate these theoretical findings, two-dimensional acoustic numerical tests are conducted, with one test successful and the other failing, indicating that both WRI and ESI can converge to the same optimum as FWI under certain conditions. Moreover, our results suggest that increasing the frequency content or sparsity can lead to these methods oscillating around the optimum.

By selectively pumping a nonlinear resonator with a coherent field, we induce a chiral interaction between the resonators, allowing us to create an all-optical diode and a three-port circulator. This chiral coupling enables our device to work with both single-photon pulses and strong light, offering an isolation ratio of over 40 dB and fidelity of more than 98%. Moreover, we've demonstrated the ability to switch nonreciprocal transmission on and off with a relatively weak pump light, effectively creating an optical transistor. Our approach provides a novel path to designing compact, chip-compatible nonreciprocal optical devices for isolating and processing quantum information.

This process is resource-intensive and, given the growing demand for video streaming, streaming service providers increasingly rely on cloud services to ensure a seamless viewing experience. As a result, video transcoding is now a significant workload on cloud services. While the performance of specific cloud services, such as GPUs or DPUs, is well-documented, the characteristics of this workload that affect cloud services' utilization and performance are less understood. This knowledge is essential to optimize cloud services' use and minimize costs. This paper investigates the application of video transcoding on cloud services, identifies the key factors that affect its performance, and proposes methods to estimate its resource requirements. Based on this research, a model is developed to predict the performance of video transcoding and validate it with multiple video streams. The results show that using this model, the accuracy of cloud resource allocation can be improved by up to 137%. The model and the analysis of video transcoding as a holistic application are then applied to a real-world video streaming use case, further validating their effectiveness.

In this study, we utilized long-term, high-speed imaging techniques to visualize zebrafish retinas in real-time during early development, aiming to investigate the underlying mechanisms governing nuclear behavior during this process. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties. This paper introduces a decision-making process to determine whether a given function is computable and, if so, to create a Turing machine that computes it. For regular functions, computability is equivalent to continuity, and the problem of determining continuity can be broken down into a specific set of criteria. This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with the ultimate goal of improving performance on tasks not yet developed.
To evaluate cross-task generalization, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes low-ratio fully supervised data as a catalyst, applying both structural and neural methods to identify functional task attributes and embed them into a shared space.

The crystallization process significantly affects a polymer's mechanical and thermal properties, necessitating consideration in both manufacturing and application design. To comprehensively capture its effects, the proposed model employs a unique decomposition of the deformation gradient and integrates a thermodynamic framework for material modeling. This framework relies on the Coleman-Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle, which in turn requires specific assumptions about the Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential. The resulting model is capable of simulating crystalline region formation and degradation, as well as temperature changes during cyclic tensile testing. By conforming to established boundary conditions and experimental evidence, it provides a framework for further investigation and validation.

For instance, in robotics, requiring the teacher to simultaneously control multiple robotic degrees of freedom to provide optimal discrete or continuous action recommendations is a complex task. The difficulty in providing optimal demonstrations limits the scope of problems that can be tackled through IL. One potential solution to this problem is to have the teacher provide corrective feedback, which is less demanding than requiring optimal demonstrations. However, current algorithms that use corrective feedback require significant modifications, incorporating parts of the teacher's feedback directly into the learning process, often at the expense of model interpretability. We introduce a novel technique for inferring optimal demonstrations from corrective feedback, without requiring any special handling of the feedback, and apply it to improve existing trajectory optimization methods. Our approach is based on a mechanism that minimizes the sum of a trained policy's action distribution against the teacher's corrective feedback, which yields an optimal action density that we approximate using a neural network. Our main contributions are a two-step process for improving the quality of the infomed model and a method that uses the infomed model to discover a better policy. Our experiments on discrete and continuous control problems demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing IL algorithms that are trained directly on raw data.

This was achieved by analyzing the noise kernels associated with the stress-energy tensor of quantum fields. In this study, we revisit this topic by employing a quantum thermodynamics approach, which involves calculating key thermodynamic parameters: heat capacity and quantum compressibility in model spacetimes with a quantum field at both high and low temperatures. This paper posits that rain generation and removal are interconnected processes that should be addressed simultaneously. To achieve this, we propose a unified image translation framework that learns to generate and remove rain simultaneously in an bidirectional manner. The framework consists of a two-way network with complementary branches that translates real rain images into clear images and vice versa. A complementary branch with a similar structure is used for each translation direction. By training the complementary branches in a bidirectional manner, the proposed framework can leverage the strength of two unidirectional models. Furthermore, we utilize contrastive learning principles to supplement the bidirectional translations, which enables the disentanglement of rain and background information. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, and it outperforms existing methods on both synthetic and real-world rain datasets.

This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) to jointly train the ASR encoder (bottom layers) and text encoder using a multi-modal learning approach. BiAM facilitates the exchange of feature sampling rates, allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in another space with diversified objective functions. Consequently, speech representations are enriched with more linguistic information, while text encoder representations become more similar to corresponding speech ones, making shared ASR models more suitable for unpaired text data pretraining. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we conduct experiments with and without extra unpaired text data, demonstrating that it can achieve a 6.15% word error rate reduction (WERR) using only paired data learning and up to 9.23% WERR when incorporating more unpaired text data, as validated on the Librispeech corpus.

unclonable encryption, a technique that prevents an adversary from creating multiple ciphertexts decrypting to the same original message. This notion is revisited, and the following points are addressed: 

- Enhancements: Previous constructions either offered one-time security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. New constructions provide unclonable encryption schemes with semantic security under minimal assumptions, available for both public-key and private-key settings.
- Limitations: The information-theoretic one-time secure construction by Broadbent and Lord was analyzed, revealing a cloning attack with a probability of success of $0.85^n$. A broader class of monogamy of entanglement games is used to generalize the construction, and a $0.75^n$ cloning attack is demonstrated against their scheme.
- Implications: Unclonable encryption satisfying a stronger property, unclonable-indistinguishability, implies copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Although current encryption schemes do not satisfy this property, this connection provides a new path to construct copy-protection.

, cutting-edge long-baseline neutrino experiments heavily rely on accurate models of neutrino interactions with atomic nuclei. These models contribute significantly to the overall systematic uncertainty due to the limited ability of existing detectors to detect final state neutrons. Next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments will incorporate three-dimensional projection scintillator trackers in their near detectors, which boast superior timing resolution and fine granularity. This technology enables the measurement of neutron kinetic energy in neutrino interactions on a per-event basis, thus providing a significant contribution to reducing the total systematic uncertainty in neutrino parameters. Prototypes of these detectors have been tested at the neutron beamline at Los Alamos National Laboratory, exposing them to neutron energies between 0 and 800 MeV in 2019 and 2020. To validate their neutron detection capabilities, the total neutron-scintillator cross section was measured and compared to external data, yielding a value of 0.36 $\pm$ 0.05 barn between 98 and 688 MeV.

This study builds upon that work by investigating how a nonlinear crystal's response is affected when it is placed in a specific optical configuration that induces a known correlation between the electric field components of light. Our results show that this scenario causes the crystal to display new phenomena, including the generation of coherent light at specific frequencies and increased amplification of certain interactions. To understand these results, we derived a new expression for the transmission of light through a nonlinear crystal and then applied it to the specific optical configuration in question. This involved making key assumptions about the crystal's properties and light's characteristics, as well as identifying a specific relationship between its properties and the optical configuration. The new expression for light transmission reveals that the crystal's response is a complex function of multiple variables, and when this is combined with the optical configuration, it leads to the generation of coherent light and increased amplification of certain interactions. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that these phenomena are caused by a coupling effect between different electric field components of light, which is influenced by the crystal's properties and the optical configuration. Additionally, our findings show that the generation of coherent light is due to a combination of phase modulation and amplitude modulation, and that the increased amplification is a result of a nonlinear process.

We do this by examining a general framework where multiple agents are instructed to act in a specific sequence, known as the action sequence. Each agent aims to maximize her value based on the actions taken by the preceding agents in the sequence. Our objective is to identify action sequences that yield nearly optimal total value to the agents, also referred to as social welfare. We assume that we have access to the value $v_i(S)$ that agent i receives when she acts after the agents in the ordered set $S$. 

We derive tight bounds on the achievable social welfare using a polynomial number of queries, even though these bounds indicate a marginally sublinear approximation of optimal social welfare in general. However, we can achieve excellent approximations when the valuations originate from a specific combinatorial domain denoted as $\mathcal{P}$, which encompasses various types of polymatroids, graph metrics, and boolean functions. Specifically, for these valuations, we can calculate social welfare using a quadratic number of queries. Moreover, we identify two scenarios where optimal social welfare can be determined efficiently: when the valuations are based on polymatroids and when they correspond to min-max functions over modular orthopolytopes. We also present a general framework for designing fair and outcome-deterministic mechanisms that cater to a broad spectrum of combinatorial optimization scenarios.

By analyzing the deformation of the Central and West African rift zone, we can infer the pre-breakup history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins. Our research indicates that the development of marginal structures like the Pre-salt sag basin and the S\~ao Paulo High is linked to changes in the direction and speed of continental extension. Initially, the rift zone experienced low-velocity, E-W extension between South America and Africa until around 126 million years ago, when rift activity in the equatorial Atlantic domain increased significantly. During this initial 17 million-year period, the Pre-salt basin width on the conjugate Brazilian and West African margins was formed. A subsequent stage, lasting from 126.06 million years to the Base Aptian period, was characterized by strain localization, rapid lithospheric weakening, and a shift in extension direction to NE-SW. The final breakup between South America and Africa occurred around 113 million years ago in the Santos-Benguela margin segment and around 103 million years ago in the Equatorial Atlantic domain. We propose that this complex rift history plays a primary role in shaping the conjugate passive margin systems and can explain the major tectonic features along the South Atlantic and possibly other passive margins.

graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete examples and mechanistic insights into this process are scarce. This study employs low-energy electron damage and helium ion irradiation to intentionally induce remote epitaxy of Pt on graphene during He+ exposure, even at moderate doses. We demonstrate that He+ ions create a persistent epittaxial interface between Pt and graphene, with unique rotational domains and epitaxial relationships. As the dose increases, Pt deposition expands, and eventually, the Pt layer forms a continuous film at higher doses. Furthermore, our findings suggest that remote epitaxy occurs through a combination of He+ ion effects and a thermal dissolution and regrowth mechanism, particularly at lower doses. The study's results also indicate that He+ ions can modulate the dissolution of graphene flakes and, consequently, the epitaxial interface. This knowledge can be applied to the design of novel heuristic methods for controlling remote epitaxy.

GeV radiation remains a mystery, and a proposed solution is the hadronic emission from magnetic arrest disks around central black holes. In these disks, particles are accelerated through magnetic reconnection and turbulence. By applying the magnetic arrest disk model to the 15 brightest radio galaxies in the GeV band, we found that it can explain their gamma-ray emission if the rate at which they consume mass is at its lowest possible speed. However, this requires a significant adjustment to the standard relativistic jet model, making it difficult to observe these gamma-rays using future telescopes studying the highest energy photons. By establishing essential mathematical equations and developing efficient algorithms, drawing on geometric and spline techniques, we calculate the probability density function, cumulative distribution function, and k-th moment of the probability function. Our tools efficiently handle large portfolios and compute high-order moments quickly, enabling realistic scenarios. We focus on the long-only strategy, where portfolios consist of non-negative weights summing to 1, and our approach can be easily generalized. By representing the stock market as a geometric simplex, we derive formulas for the first four moments of the cross-sectional returns distribution and develop an algorithm for computing higher moments. Furthermore, we apply our portfolio return theory to design more effective risk management strategies, finding that the cross-sectional returns distribution is skewed to the left and asset returns are negatively related to the coefficient of variation.

cardiac auscultation is a vital point-of-care method. However, the automatic analysis of heart sounds faces significant challenges due to noise and sensor degradation. research focuses on the process of producing leptoquark pairs at the Large Hadron Collider with an emphasis on its potential to provide precise constraints on leptoquark parameters and aid in identifying these sources of new physics. The unique characteristic of this process, referred to as asymmetric pair production, involves the creation of two distinct leptoquarks through proton-proton collisions facilitated by a lepton exchange, where the produced leptoquarks are not their own charge conjugates. To ensure the feasibility of this process, we outline the necessary conditions and identify potential combinations of leptoquark multiplets that can give rise to it. Furthermore, we conduct several phenomenological studies within the context of simplified scalar leptoquark extensions of the Standard Model to demonstrate how to incorporate asymmetric pair production into the reinterpretation of existing experimental data, thereby obtaining accurate constraints on leptoquark parameters.

Existing methods are primarily designed for either time series or sequence analysis, despite the increasing interest in temporal sequence data. For instance, spectral transforms are used to retain key information while eliminating noise, while features are usually selected or a model is fitted along the time course. Nevertheless, conventional numerical solutions of the SWEs are computationally intensive and require precise riverbed profile measurements. We present a two-step approach to address this issue. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes a novel energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed framework, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration.

Reinforcement learning models struggle to generalize and adapt when faced with new tasks beyond their training data, driving interest in the development of continual learning algorithms. To advance this research, there is a need for carefully crafted challenge environments, experiments, and evaluation metrics. To address this need, we introduce L2Explorer, a Unity-based, 3D exploration environment that can be dynamically reconfigured to create diverse tasks and task variations within complex, evolving evaluation curricula. This paper investigates a two-level ecosystem consisting of two predator species competing for a common prey, incorporating explicit interference competition. By adjusting the system, we create a singular perturbation model that separates into a fast and a slow component. The fast component represents short-term ecosystem interactions, while the slow component captures long-term dynamics influenced by the regime shifts. Near a singularly perturbed equilibrium, the system's behavior is analyzed within both near-equilibrium and asymptotic regimes. Specifically, the slow dynamics within the interior of the equilibrium's basin of attraction is characterized by a strong Allee effect, which ensures the system's stability. Furthermore, the paper introduces an ordinary differential equation model to capture the fast dynamics at the edge of a regime shift, focusing on the prey's invasion dynamics. The study reveals that the ecosystem is stable against prey invasions when the large predator is present, but a sudden decline in the large predator population can lead to a regime shift and the emergence of a new equilibrium. However, if the prey population grows sufficiently before the second predator species invasions, the system will converge to a new equilibrium with the two predator species and a reduced prey population.

However, these protocols lead to memory instruction reordering, resulting in additional, unrelated instructions. This phenomenon is referred to as coherent memory access reordering. A theoretical and practical analysis of coherent memory access reordering is presented, focusing on its source, semantics, and potential impact on instruction streams. A key observation is the existence of a fixed point in the protocol, allowing for the prediction of all possible coherent memory access reorders before system initialization. This enables the development of an optimal, static strategy for reordering-aware program compilation, yielding better instruction scheduling efficiency without compromising safety. Experimental results, based on the NUI Galway Cache Model, demonstrate a 13% improvement in program instruction density. The protocol itself remains unchanged, and there are no adjustments required for existing programs, utilizing existing binary formats and execution environments.

Each of these galaxies has a compact, star-bursting core surrounded by a massive, disk-like structure. What's surprising is that these disks are both inactive and severely unevenly distributed. This suggests that these galaxies are experiencing a type of quenching that begins from the outside in. We propose that the unevenness in the disks, likely caused by the effects of accreted gas and interactions with nearby stars, has triggered the development of massive, star-forming clumps. As these galaxies navigate the complex dynamics of their group, the disks are being stretched and distorted, while the compact cores remain overactive. Once a galaxy's massive clumps have consumed all the available fuel, its disk will collapse, and a smaller, inactive core will form, resulting in the phenomenon of outside-in quenching. This process is expected to be the dominant mechanism of galaxy quenching, particularly in the early stages of cosmic structure formation.

A key feature of the UTZ model is its ability to consistently predict the small ratios of fermion masses by incorporating a minimal set of new physical parameters. In our revised version, we remove the reliance on symmetry arguments that previously drove the UTZ's unique flavour structure. Additionally, we explore the various possibilities for explaining the long-standing issues surrounding the $\mu$ problem.

This research introduces a novel approach to resolving this dilemma by re-examining the foregone conclusion doctrine, a concept rooted in Fisher v US. Our objective is to develop a framework that enables courts to determine whether any action implies knowledge already possessed by the government. This paper presents a more focused approach, proposing a framework that identifies actions where all implicit testimony can be considered a foregone conclusion. Our approach places the burden on the government to prove it is not relying on the defendant's truthful response. Building on legal and computer science theories, we introduce the concept of demonstrability as a central idea in evaluating compelled actions. We also develop a language to assess whether a compelled action allows the respondent to achieve the government's desired outcome in an equivalent manner. Our framework is applied to analyze the compellability of various cryptographic primitives and password entry methods. Notably, we arrive at a general conclusion that compels a respondent to disclose password information to the government, whereas physical access to the device remains a matter of judicial discretion.

Analysis of spectroscopic data for KIC 9267654 reveals a significant surface rotation variation, consistent with an oblique rotary effect, causing the rotation period to appear different in different spectral lines. Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) is used to treat a specific type of epilepsy by destroying affected brain areas. A novel approach called the Resource-Expedient Epilepsy Lesion Segmentation (RAELS) network addresses this issue by incorporating prior knowledge and using fewer training images while maintaining high performance. RAELS's results are comparable to existing networks, but with significantly fewer training data, making it an invaluable tool for researchers and clinicians working with LITT data.
